shortlist.raw_text: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

shortlist.raw_text: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

Title: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial

Article text (excerpt):
LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team.
The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change?
According to the Financial Times , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions.

KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised.
The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged.
Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow.
The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation.
The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts.
Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks.
KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively.
The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial.
Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions.
For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information.
However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees.
The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism.
There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used.
The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise.
For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does.

A top reader comment on Hacker News (opinion, not fact):
I suspect this says more about KPMG accountants than AI.
text:
More than 100 AI agents audited a major UK company alongside KPMG.

Several times, the machines dug deeper and asked better questions than the human team.

That finding comes from Project Exponential.

KPMG UK tested the agents on the accounts of an unnamed FTSE 250 company over a four-month period.

The software handled tasks across the entire audit workflow:
• collecting information
• analyzing and documenting data
• drafting conclusions
• suggesting subsequent steps

Human oversight was still required. An auditor had to step in when one agent failed to match regulatory requirements with company documentation.

KPMG plans to expand the trial to 20 larger audits.

My read: the economic model of accounting relies on large teams of junior staff doing repetitive analysis. When autonomous agents can do that work deeper and faster, the billable hour starts to break down.

The limitation is strict. The trial was not a formally approved statutory audit, data quality remains an obstacle, and the technology is not yet ready for thousands of engagements.

How many junior audit roles disappear when the software starts asking better questions than the staff?

Source: europeanbusinessmagazine.com
alt_openings:
1. Shape: Bare number first
Opening: Four months. Over 100 AI agents. One FTSE 250 company audit.
Deepening line: The machines ended up asking better questions than KPMG's human accountants.
When to prefer it: Use when the raw scale of the test is the most arresting thing in the material.

2. Shape: Corrective
Opening: AI in finance does not just speed up administrative tasks anymore.
Deepening line: It now investigates financial issues more deeply than human audit teams.
When to prefer it: Use when readers likely assume the tool is still just a glorified calculator.

3. Shape: Your X
Opening: Your next corporate audit may be challenged by software that outperforms junior staff.
Deepening line: KPMG found that AI agents running accounts analysis asked questions human auditors missed.
When to prefer it: Use when you want to hook professional services readers directly through their own business model.

Pick: The tool-as-subject opening ("More than 100 AI agents audited a major UK company...") because it immediately sets up the unusual contrast between human professionals and machine software without giving away the outcome.
